newsitem.title: USA: Utilities seek review of NY competition order.
newsitem.headline: Utilities seek review of NY competition order.

text.p: Eight New York utilities have gone to court to seek a review of the state Public Service Commission's May 20 "Competitive Opportunities" order, the Energy Association of New York State said.

The association said it joined its member companies on Wednesday to file a suit in New York State Supreme Court in Albany challenging the commission's May 20th order to restructure the electric utility industry.
"We support the general thrust of the PSC's order, said Niagara Mohawk Power Corp chief executive William Davis said.
"However, we want to protect our legal rights until all issues related to competition in New York are settled fairly."
The association said the suit was filed pursuant to Article 78 of New York's Civil Practice Law and Rules, which requires such petitions to be submitted within four months.

The association's other members are Brooklyn Union Gas Co, Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp, Consolidated Edison Co of New York Inc, Long Island Lighting Co, New York State Electric & Gas Corp, Orange and Rockland Utilities Inc and Rochester Gas and Electric Corp.
"Discussions with the Department of Public Service and other interested parties will continue with respect to important restructuring issues," said Howard Shapiro, Energy Association president.

"However, were we to let the filing deadline pass, we could waive our legal rights to challenge certain aspects of the May 20th order. This proceeding does not challenge competition." The Energy Association said the suit contends the May 20th order does not guarantee service reliability, fair treatment of concerned parties and a level playing field for all participants.
In a separate statement, NYSEG said it will comply with the commission's October 1 deadline for filing a detailed plan to bring wholesale and retail competition to its service area.
"We also want to ensure that lawful investments made to serve customers are protected," said Jack H. Roskoz, NYSEG's executive vice president, referring to what are commonly called stranded costs.
